title: The stone bridge
hook: Zhaozhou's bridge lets donkeys and horses cross: a teaching for everyone (Blue Cliff Record 52)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the top of a hundred-foot pole, and the call to take one more step. Your line: step off the pole. What small step past comfort did you take? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven, and a new week begins.

A monk has heard, for a long time, about a stone bridge at Zhaozhou. So when he finally arrives to meet the teacher who shares the town's name, he can't resist a little jab. I've heard so much about the stone bridge of Zhaozhou, he says. Now that I'm here, all I see is a plain log bridge. It's a pun, and a challenge: the great teacher looks ordinary up close. Zhaozhou doesn't get defensive. He plays along. Today's case comes from a different collection, the Blue Cliff Record, case fifty-two.
screen: `A FAMOUS STONE BRIDGE.` → `ALL I SEE IS A LOG.` → `ZHAOZHOU PLAYS ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the collection. Until now these koan days drew on the Gateless Gate. The Blue Cliff Record is another collection, with its own cases, verses and commentary, and Zhaozhou turns up in both. The cypress tree, two days ago, was his too. Second, the exchange. In paraphrase: the monk says he sees only a log bridge. Zhaozhou answers, you see the log bridge, but you don't see the stone bridge. The monk takes the bait: then what is the stone bridge? And Zhaozhou says: donkeys cross, horses cross. Third, what the answer opens up. A bridge doesn't check who's walking on it. It doesn't ask donkeys to be horses, or horses to be monks. It carries whatever comes. Some readers hear Zhaozhou describing his own way of teaching: it isn't grand to look at, but anyone can get across on it. In that reading, the plain log the monk sneered at and the stone bridge he'd heard about are the same thing seen two ways. Fourth, why it's gentle. The monk came to test the teacher and expose him as ordinary. Zhaozhou doesn't deny the log. He says the monk hasn't seen the stone bridge yet, and then describes it in the plainest words he has. A bridge you notice is one that hasn't quite done its job yet. A good bridge disappears under your feet. You're on the other side before you think about it. There's a quiet humility here, and a wide welcome: whatever kind of traveler arrives, the bridge holds.
screen: `A SECOND COLLECTION: THE BLUE CLIFF.` · `YOU DON'T SEE THE STONE BRIDGE.` · `DONKEYS CROSS, HORSES CROSS.` · `A GOOD BRIDGE DISAPPEARS.` · then, large: `DONKEYS CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath carry itself, the way a bridge carries traffic, without choosing. Bring to mind one thing you've made or know how to do: a recipe, a skill, a spare room, a bit of knowledge. Then think of someone who could use it, someone you might not have picked. Picture them crossing on it, getting where they need to go. Let that be enough. No thanks needed. When the mind drifts, come back to the breath, carrying whatever comes. The bell holds the time.
The stone bridge. Zhaozhou's answer in case fifty-two of the Blue Cliff Record: what is the stone bridge? Donkeys cross, horses cross. A teaching anyone can walk on. Today's word.
Your line: donkeys cross. Today, let one person use something you made or know, without checking whether they deserve it. Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: The Blue Cliff Record is studied in Rinzai Zen training alongside the Gateless Gate; its cases, with their verses and commentary, are given as koans and also taken up in teachers' talks.

fork.setup: you're Zhaozhou. a visiting monk says your stone bridge looks like a plain log up close. how do you reply?
options: say he sees the log but not the stone bridge, and say what crosses on it.
fork.reveal: Zhaozhou says the monk sees the log but not the stone bridge, and when asked what the stone bridge is: donkeys cross, horses cross.

original.note: Chinese: 'donkeys cross, horses cross', Zhaozhou's answer. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a bridge.
what it means: a plain teaching that carries whoever comes, donkey or horse.
what a scholar hears: Blue Cliff Record case 52, a pun on the town's stone bridge and Zhaozhou's name, answered with du lü du ma.

notes: New week begins at day 1247 (after week-end day 1246).

Case 52 paraphrased. Confirm: monk has long heard of Zhaozhou's stone bridge but sees only a log (or simple plank) bridge; Zhaozhou: you see the log bridge, you don't see the stone bridge; monk: what is the stone bridge? Zhaozhou: donkeys cross, horses cross.
'Heard so much about' paraphrases the monk's own words ('I've long heard of'); no claim about the real bridge's history is made.
'A good bridge disappears under your feet' and the humility/welcome reading are interpretation; 'readers often hear' softened as a reading.
Attribution of the Blue Cliff Record (Xuedou's verses, Yuanwu's commentary) given only in sources; confirm. Original 渡驢渡馬: confirm.

Editor pass: corrected the claim that Zhaozhou 'agrees' he is ordinary (he says the monk sees the log but not the stone bridge), in the teach and the fork option; 'readers often hear' softened to 'some readers'.
